tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA data center revenue H100 H200 split Q2 FY2027 earnings call

events.content: NVIDIA data center revenue H100 H200 split Q2 FY2027 earnings call

**NVIDIA Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion in Q2 FY2027** (quarter ended July 26, 2026), increasing **18% sequentially** and **117% year over year**; it represented about **92.5%** of total company revenue of $96.2 billion. [[1]]

**Primary growth drivers**

- **Blackwell Ultra infrastructure ramp:** NVIDIA’s 10-Q identifies the ramp of Blackwell Ultra as the direct driver of Data Center growth, while Blackwell accounted for the majority of system shipments. [[2]]
- **Broad hyperscaler demand:** Hyperscale Data Center revenue reached **$48.7 billion**, up **13% QoQ** and **102% YoY**, driven by sustained strength in Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra deployments. [[2]]
- **Faster growth outside traditional hyperscalers:** AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise (“ACIE”) revenue rose to **$40.3 billion**, up **25% QoQ** and **138% YoY**, pointing to incremental demand from neoclouds, AI-model makers, industrial customers, and enterprises. [[2, 3]]
- **AI-infrastructure buildout widened across customer types:** NVIDIA characterized demand as extending across hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native firms, enterprises, and sovereign customers, supported by an expanding global AI-infrastructure buildout. [[3]]
- **More valuable full-system content per gigawatt:** NVIDIA’s platform extends beyond GPUs to CPUs, NVLink, and InfiniBand/Ethernet networking; management said the revenue opportunity increased from roughly **$18 billion/GW for Hopper** to **$25 billion/GW for Grace Blackwell**, increasing revenue content as customers deploy AI factories. [[3]]
- **China was not material to the result:** Hopper Data Center sales to China were less than **1% of Data Center revenue** in the quarter, so the growth was principally generated elsewhere. [[2]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 FY2027 growth was not solely a unit-volume rebound—it reflected the Blackwell Ultra product-cycle ramp, accelerating purchases by hyperscalers, outsized expansion in neocloud/enterprise/industrial demand, and higher platform content per AI data-center deployment. [[2, 3]]

Sources:
[S9.1] NVIDIA Corporation - NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Second Quarter Fiscal 2027 — https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Announces-Financial-Results-for-Second-Quarter-Fiscal-2027/default.aspx

tool_arguments.query: AMD Instinct GPU revenue 2025 full year data center

events.content: AMD Instinct GPU revenue 2025 full year data center

AMD does not separately report a full annual revenue line for **AMD Instinct data-center GPUs**, so a precise 2024–2025 Instinct GPU growth rate cannot be calculated from disclosed figures. [[1, 2]] 

The clearest disclosed figure is that Instinct accelerator revenue exceeded **$5 billion in FY2024**, following the MI300 launch and ramp; AMD characterized the product as having ramped in 2024 rather than publishing a comparable FY2023 Instinct-only revenue figure. [[1, 3]] 

As the broader, reported proxy, AMD’s Data Center revenue rose from **$6.5 billion in FY2023** to **$12.6 billion in FY2024**, a **94% year-over-year increase**, driven by both Instinct GPUs and EPYC server CPUs. [[4, 1]] 

In FY2025, Data Center revenue increased another **32% to $16.6 billion**, while AMD said Instinct GPU revenue reached a record, driven by the MI350-series ramp and expanding customer engagements; however, it again did not disclose the Instinct-only dollar total or growth percentage. [[5, 2]] 

Quarterly momentum also remained positive in 2025: Data Center revenue was **$4.3 billion in Q3 2025 (+22% YoY)** and **$5.4 billion in Q4 2025 (+39% YoY)**, with AMD attributing growth partly to Instinct MI350 shipments. [[6, 5]]

**Bottom line:** Instinct GPU revenue scaled from an early MI300 launch/ramp in 2023 to **more than $5 billion in 2024**, and reached another record in 2025, while the encompassing Data Center segment expanded from **$6.5 billion to $12.6 billion to $16.6 billion** across FY2023–FY2025. [[3, 1, 2, 4, 5]]

private_messages.content:
**NVIDIA Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion in Q2 FY2027** (quarter ended July 26, 2026), increasing **18% sequentially** and **117% year over year**; it represented about **92.5%** of total company revenue of $96.2 billion. [[1]]

**Primary growth drivers**

- **Blackwell Ultra infrastructure ramp:** NVIDIA’s 10-Q identifies the ramp of Blackwell Ultra as the direct driver of Data Center growth, while Blackwell accounted for the majority of system shipments. [[2]]
- **Broad hyperscaler demand:** Hyperscale Data Center revenue reached **$48.7 billion**, up **13% QoQ** and **102% YoY**, driven by sustained strength in Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra deployments. [[2]]
- **Faster growth outside traditional hyperscalers:** AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise (“ACIE”) revenue rose to **$40.3 billion**, up **25% QoQ** and **138% YoY**, pointing to incremental demand from neoclouds, AI-model makers, industrial customers, and enterprises. [[2, 3]]
- **AI-infrastructure buildout widened across customer types:** NVIDIA characterized demand as extending across hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native firms, enterprises, and sovereign customers, supported by an expanding global AI-infrastructure buildout. [[3]]
- **More valuable full-system content per gigawatt:** NVIDIA’s platform extends beyond GPUs to CPUs, NVLink, and InfiniBand/Ethernet networking; management said the revenue opportunity increased from roughly **$18 billion/GW for Hopper** to **$25 billion/GW for Grace Blackwell**, increasing revenue content as customers deploy AI factories. [[3]]
- **China was not material to the result:** Hopper Data Center sales to China were less than **1% of Data Center revenue** in the quarter, so the growth was principally generated elsewhere. [[2]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 FY2027 growth was not solely a unit-volume rebound—it reflected the Blackwell Ultra product-cycle ramp, accelerating purchases by hyperscalers, outsized expansion in neocloud/enterprise/industrial demand, and higher platform content per AI data-center deployment. [[2, 3]]
